**Galactic outflows and feedback** refer to the large-scale, energetic ejection of gas and heavy [[chemical-elements|Chemical elements]] from a galaxy's [[cosmic-media-and-interstellar-medium|Cosmic Media and Interstellar Medium]] into the surrounding [[circumgalactic-medium|Circumgalactic Medium]] and intergalactic space. In modern cosmological paradigms, these processes are strictly necessary to resolve the [[overcooling-problem|Overcooling problem]]—the theoretical tendency for gas in dark matter halos to cool too efficiently, which would otherwise result in catastrophic runaway star formation and cosmic stellar mass densities far exceeding observational constraints [Hopkins et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011MNRAS.417..950H/abstract). To establish [[self-regulated-feedback-mechanisms|Self-regulated feedback mechanisms]], galaxies rely on continuous energy and momentum injection from two primary macroscopic drivers: [[stellar-and-agn-feedback|Stellar and AGN Feedback]]. In low-mass systems, pre-supernova ionizing radiation and supernova explosions from [[massive-stars|Massive stars]] dominate the regulation of the interstellar medium. Conversely, in [[massive-galaxies|Massive galaxies]] residing in halos above $M_{\rm halo} \gtrsim 10^{12} M_\odot$, mechanical jets and radiation from [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]] take over as the primary engines preventing runaway accretion and maintaining quiescence [Fabian et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012ARA&A..50..455F/abstract).

Structurally, [[superwinds|galactic winds]] are not uniform streams but rather a complex [[multiphase-wind|Multiphase wind]] phenomenon. They consist of a hot, X-ray emitting plasma that carries the bulk of the thermal energy and newly synthesized metals, which simultaneously entrains cooler warm-ionized, neutral, and dense molecular phases that often dominate the total expelled mass and momentum [Sturm et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011ApJ...733L..16S/abstract). The efficiency of this gas removal is typically parameterized by the [[mass-loading-factor|Mass loading factor]], which describes the ratio of the mass outflow rate to the star formation rate [Muratov et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015MNRAS.454.2691M/abstract), [Sugahara et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ApJ...850...51S/abstract). By driving [[chemical-enrichment-and-metal-transport|Chemical Enrichment and Metal Transport]] into the halo, these outflows establish the fundamental mass-metallicity scaling relations observed across cosmic time. Furthermore, much of this ejected material does not escape the dark matter halo permanently; instead, it cools and re-accretes via [[galactic-fountains|Galactic fountains]], driving a continuous cycle of [[wind-recycling|Wind recycling]] that supplies the [[net-gas-inflows|Net gas inflows]] required for late-time star formation.

The impact of these outflows on galaxy evolution is conventionally viewed through the lens of [[negative-feedback|Negative feedback]], wherein the depletion and heating of gas reservoirs quench star formation [King et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015ARA&A..53..115K/abstract), [Nesvadba et al. (2006)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2006ApJ...650..693N/abstract). However, recent observational and theoretical advances reveal a highly nuanced picture that includes [[positive-feedback-astrophysics|Positive feedback (astrophysics)]], where outflow-driven shocks and radio jets compress dense gas and locally trigger starbursts. This article explores the fundamental drivers and multiphase structures of galactic winds, tracing the historical development of feedback models and their corresponding scaling relations. Finally, it highlights pressing open questions in the field, including severe observational tensions regarding the true coupling efficiency of feedback in local dwarf galaxies, the uncertain thermodynamic role of cosmic rays, and the extent to which early-universe feedback transitioned from a primarily positive, turbulence-driving mechanism to the ejective, negative quenching seen in massive galaxies today.

## Fundamental Drivers: Stellar and AGN Feedback

To maintain the self-regulated balance described above, galaxies depend on [[multi-scale-feedback-processes|multi-scale energy injection]]. On the scales of star-forming disks, this regulation is primarily mediated by [[massive-stars|Massive stars]]. High-resolution simulations tracking individual stellar populations demonstrate that pre-supernova feedback—specifically [[radiation-driven-winds|Radiation-driven winds]], photoionization, and [[radiation-pressure|Radiation pressure]]—is critical for clearing dense gas in [[molecular-clouds-and-gas-clumping|giant molecular clouds]] within $\sim 1-3$ Myr of star formation [Emerick et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018ApJ...865L..22E/abstract), [Chevance et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022MNRAS.509..272C/abstract). This early dispersal of the local [[cosmic-media-and-interstellar-medium|interstellar medium (ISM)]] drastically reduces the surrounding gas density, preventing severe radiative losses of the subsequent supernova energy. Consequently, supernova-driven winds can efficiently break out of the galactic disk, launching [[multiphase-wind|multiphase outflows]] that carry significant mass and metals into the [[circumgalactic-medium|Circumgalactic Medium]] [Agertz et al. (2014)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015ApJ...804...18A/abstract), [Li et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...890L..30L/abstract). 

The efficiency of these outflows is typically quantified by the [[mass-loading-factor|Mass loading factor]], defined as $\eta = \dot{M}_{\rm out}/\mathrm{SFR}$. Analytical frameworks and cosmological simulations suggest that $\eta$ scales inversely with the host halo's circular velocity, $v_c$. This scaling often follows $\eta \propto v_c^{-1}$ for [[momentum-driven-feedback-mechanisms|Momentum-driven Feedback Mechanisms]] or $\eta \propto v_c^{-2}$ for energy-driven flows [Sugahara et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ApJ...850...51S/abstract), [Mitchell et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.494.3971M/abstract). While highly elevated mass-loading factors ($\eta \sim 10-100$) are requisite in simulations to match the faint end of the stellar mass function, observational tensions persist. For instance, highly resolved kinematics of nearby dwarf galaxies occasionally infer much lower mass-loading factors ($\eta \sim 0.02$), suggesting that [[stellar-and-agn-feedback|stellar feedback]] may sometimes stimulate a gentle gas cycle rather than a catastrophic blowout [Marasco et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023A&A...670A..92M/abstract).

In [[massive-galaxies|Massive galaxies]] ($M_{\rm halo} \gtrsim 10^{12} M_\odot$), the gravitational potential is too deep for stellar feedback to unbind significant gas. Furthermore, theoretical studies show that non-AGN mechanisms—such as Type Ia supernovae, cosmic ray feedback, and morphological quenching—are entirely insufficient to halt cooling flows in halos above this threshold [Su et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019MNRAS.487.4393S/abstract). Here, the dominant driver of feedback transitions to [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]] [Fabian et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012ARA&A..50..455F/abstract), [King et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015ARA&A..53..115K/abstract). AGN feedback operates via two primary channels. In the "quasar mode," which occurs at high accretion rates, radiation pressure acting directly on the obscuring dust drives massive, wide-angle [[molecular-winds|Molecular winds]] and ionized [[x-ray-winds|X-ray winds]] [Ishibashi et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016MNRAS.463.1291I/abstract), [Barnes et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.494.1143B/abstract). These outflows can launch as ultra-fast outflows (UFOs) with [[mildly-relativistic-outflows|mildly relativistic velocities]] of $v \sim 0.1-0.2c$ [King et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015ARA&A..53..115K/abstract). Conversely, the "radio mode" relies on [[mechanical-feedback|Mechanical feedback]] from highly collimated, relativistic jets. These jets interact heavily with the ISM and the surrounding halo, inflating massive X-ray cavities, driving shocks, and uplifting metal-rich gas to maintain the thermal balance of the hot halo over long timescales [Ciotti et al. (2010)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010ApJ...717..708C/abstract), [Duan et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018ApJ...861..106D/abstract). Consequently, full AGN feedback prescriptions in modern numerical simulations, such as the FEGA25 model, must dynamically coordinate negative, positive, and hot gas-ejection modes to efficiently expel gas beyond the virial radius, precisely matching observed [[gas-fraction|halo gas fractions]] [Contini et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ApJS..279...18C/abstract).

## Stellar Feedback and Pre-Supernova Processes

Traditionally, supernova (SN) explosions were considered the primary regulators of galactic gas dynamics. However, modern high-resolution simulations (such as FIRE-2 and SMUGGLE) and multi-wavelength observations demonstrate that [[strong-pre-sn-feedback|Strong pre-SN feedback]] is critical for establishing realistic [[star-formation-processes|Star Formation Processes]] and baryon cycles. Pre-supernova mechanisms—chiefly [[stellar-ionizing-radiation|Stellar ionizing radiation]], [[radiation-pressure|Radiation pressure]], and mechanical [[stellar-feedback-and-winds|stellar winds]] from [[massive-stars|Massive stars]]—inject essential momentum and energy into the [[cosmic-media-and-interstellar-medium|ISM]] long before the first [[sn-feedback-model|SN detonations]] occur.

Within [[molecular-clouds-and-gas-clumping|giant molecular clouds (GMCs)]], UV photons from young massive stars create expanding HII regions through photoionization and Lyman-Werner dissociation of molecular hydrogen. This [[stellar-ionizing-radiation|Stellar ionizing radiation]] provides immediate, localized pressure that disrupts the dense gas environment. Simulations indicate that H$_2$-dissociating radiation and photoionization are crucial for suppressing runaway star formation and reproducing the observed Kennicutt-Schmidt relation without artificial fine-tuning [Butler et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ApJ...841...82B/abstract). Consequently, GMCs are typically dispersed rapidly, within $\sim 1-3$ Myr after the emergence of unembedded high-mass stars [Chevance et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022MNRAS.509..272C/abstract).

The dynamical impact of these early feedback channels is profound. In models of low-mass dwarf galaxies, tracking ionizing radiation explicitly with adaptive ray-tracing has been shown to reduce the global star formation rate by over a factor of 5 [Emerick et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018ApJ...865L..22E/abstract). Furthermore, the dominant physical driver depends heavily on the galactic environment: [[radiation-pressure|Radiation pressure]] is the primary wind-driving mechanism in massive, gas-rich starbursts at high redshift, whereas shock-heated gas from SNe and stellar winds dominates in Milky Way-like and dwarf systems [Hopkins et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.421.3522H/abstract). By limiting the dense gas reservoir, combined pre-SN mechanisms self-regulate the local [[average-star-formation-efficiency|star formation efficiency]] per free-fall time to $\varepsilon_{\rm ff} \approx 10\%$, closely matching observational estimates in molecular clouds [Agertz et al. (2014)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015ApJ...804...18A/abstract).

Crucially, [[strong-pre-sn-feedback|Strong pre-SN feedback]] acts as a prerequisite for efficient SN-driven outflows. By evacuating dense gas and carving low-density channels through the ISM, early feedback limits the catastrophic radiative cooling of subsequent SN remnants. This allows the SN thermal energy to efficiently escape the natal cloud and drive large-scale, [[multiphase-wind|multiphase]] [[galaxy-outflows|galactic winds]] into the [[circumgalactic-medium|Circumgalactic Medium]] [Lucas et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.493.4700L/abstract).

Despite a consensus on its necessity, the precise efficiency of energy coupling remains an area of active debate. Observations and analytical models suggest that the mechanical and radiative coupling efficiency to the parent GMC is relatively low—often only a few tens of percent—meaning the vast majority of the injected momentum and energy escapes into the broader ISM rather than acting on the cloud itself [Chevance et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022MNRAS.509..272C/abstract). Additionally, the literature conflicts on the broader impact of early stellar kinematics. While runaway stars might theoretically be expected to spread SN feedback into more diffuse [[extra-planar-and-circumgalactic-gas|extra-planar gas]], high-resolution models indicate they have a surprisingly weak net impact in dwarf galaxies, as the ISM has already been rendered highly porous by early pre-SN feedback [Andersson et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023MNRAS.521.2196A/abstract).

## AGN Feedback: Quasar and Radio Modes

In models of galaxy formation, feedback from [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|supermassive black holes]] is widely invoked to solve the [[overcooling-problem|Overcooling problem]] and regulate star formation in [[massive-galaxies|Massive galaxies]] (halo masses $M > 10^{12} M_\odot$). This regulation is broadly partitioned into two regimes: the "quasar" (or radiative) mode and the "radio" (or kinetic/jet) mode. These modes couple energy and momentum to the ISM and the [[circumgalactic-medium|Circumgalactic Medium]] (CGM) through distinct physical mechanisms. Indeed, observations show that approximately 60% of all AGNs across many orders of magnitude in luminosity exhibit intrinsic outflows [Ganguly et al. (2007)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2008ApJ...672..102G/abstract).

**The Quasar Mode (Radiative Feedback)**
The quasar mode operates during periods of radiatively efficient accretion, typically when the supermassive black hole is accreting near the Eddington limit. Feedback in this regime is driven by [[radiation-pressure|Radiation pressure]]—often coupled to dust grains [Ishibashi et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016MNRAS.463.1291I/abstract)—and by Compton and photoionization heating. This intense radiation field can launch highly ionized [[x-ray-winds|X-ray winds]] and ultra-fast outflows (UFOs) from the inner accretion disk, reaching [[mildly-relativistic-outflows|mildly relativistic velocities]] of $v \sim 0.1 - 0.2c$ [King et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015ARA&A..53..115K/abstract), [Luminari et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018A&A...619A.149L/abstract). Moreover, the kinetic energy in ionized outflows often constitutes a surprisingly large fraction of the total AGN power, functioning as a fundamental [[negative-feedback|Negative feedback]] mechanism that is observationally detected in at least 50% of nearby AGNs [Laha et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021NatAs...5...13L/abstract). A recent meta-analysis of over 100 UFO detections establishes strong correlations between line width, equivalent width, and velocity, robustly supporting clumpy, multi-component wind models in these inner regions [Laurenti et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251206077L/abstract). Furthermore, theoretical models demonstrate that incorporating observationally calibrated X-ray radiation fields from AGN can be twice as effective as local thermal energy injection at suppressing long-term star formation [Hambrick et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011ApJ...738...16H/abstract). Recent cosmological implementations of these winds, such as the MISTRAL stochastic bipolar momentum feedback model, have successfully suppressed star formation and regulated gas fractions across diverse halo masses explicitly without relying on ad-hoc mass-dependent scalings [Farcy et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.543..967F/abstract).

Despite the vast kinetic power of quasar-driven winds, the literature exhibits significant tension regarding their spatial reach and global quenching efficiency. Some integral field spectroscopy studies find that the mass and kinetic energy of ionized outflows are largely confined to the central kiloparsec of the host galaxy, resulting in energy conversion efficiencies of only $0.01\% - 1\%$. This observation casts doubt on the ability of these outflows to exert instantaneous, galaxy-scale [[negative-feedback|Negative feedback]] [Karouzos et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016ApJ...833..171K/abstract). In contrast, other observational campaigns suggest that while immediate, global suppression of star formation may be limited, the long-term, delayed effects of these outflows are sufficient to eventually deplete the host's star-forming gas reservoir [Luo et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021ApJ...908..221L/abstract). 

**The Radio Mode (Kinetic Feedback)**
At lower accretion rates, AGN feedback transitions into the radio or kinetic mode, which is the primary quenching maintenance mechanism in massive elliptical galaxies and galaxy clusters. This mode is characterized by collimated relativistic jets that provide [[mechanical-feedback|Mechanical feedback]] to the host's environment. [[radio-galaxy-explosions|Radio galaxy explosions]] and the continuous injection of jet plasma inflate buoyant cavities and bubbles in the hot halo, shock-heating the ambient gas and preventing it from cooling and accreting onto the galaxy [Fabian et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012ARA&A..50..455F/abstract). Interestingly, surveys such as MaNGA indicate that radio-detected AGNs exhibit higher outflow velocities and momentum rates compared to radio-undetected sources, even though radiation remains the primary physical driver of these warm ionized gas outflows on larger scales [Nandi et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ApJ...984...20N/abstract). Even in systems hosting relatively low-power radio jets, surveys such as MAGNUM have revealed significant ionized gas turmoil and shocks driven into the ISM perpendicular to the jet axis, further illustrating the complex multi-directional impact of jet-ISM interactions [Venturi et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021A&A...648A..17V/abstract).

High-resolution hydrodynamic simulations indicate that to match the observed X-ray luminosities and stellar masses of elliptical galaxies, the energy coupling efficiency of this mechanical feedback must be relatively low, on the order of $\epsilon \sim 10^{-4}$ [Ciotti et al. (2010)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010ApJ...717..708C/abstract). Despite this low global efficiency, radio-mode feedback operates over immense spatial scales. Jet-driven bubbles can uplift metal-rich gas from the galactic core out to distances exceeding $100\text{ kpc}$ via hydrodynamic "Darwin drift" [Duan et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018ApJ...861..106D/abstract). Furthermore, cosmological simulations demonstrate that long-range jet feedback is essential to reproduce the column density distribution of the low-redshift Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, highlighting its profound impact on the [[cosmic-media-and-interstellar-medium|intergalactic medium]] [Tillman et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...945L..17T/abstract).

## Multiphase Outflow Structure

Galactic outflows are inherently a [[multiphase-wind|Multiphase wind]] phenomenon, consisting of gas that spans several orders of magnitude in temperature and density. Observations across a wide range of redshifts and host galaxy types—including starbursts and AGNs—consistently reveal a complex structure comprising hot X-ray emitting plasma, warm ionized gas, neutral atomic gas, and cold molecular material [Rupke et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018Galax...6..138R/abstract), [Ponti et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021A&A...646A..66P/abstract).

The hot phase ($T \approx 10^{6-7}$ K), generated by the thermalization of supernova ejecta or AGN winds, acts as the primary energetic driver of the outflow. While it may not dominate the total mass budget, the hot phase carries the vast majority of the outflow's energy and newly synthesized metals [Li et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...898..148L/abstract). Simulations indicate that the specific energy of the hot outflow is $10-1000$ times higher than that of the cooler phases, and its kinematics dictate the eventual metal enrichment of the [[circumgalactic-medium|Circumgalactic Medium]] [Li et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...890L..30L/abstract). The warm ionized component, frequently studied via optical emission lines (e.g., [O III]) and [[warm-absorber-outflows|Warm absorber outflows]] in the UV/X-ray, typically traces gas at $T \sim 10^4$ K. However, calculating the global [[ionised-mass-outflow-rate|Ionised Mass Outflow Rate]] requires careful modeling of the gas density profile, as different density estimators can yield mass outflow rates that vary by orders of magnitude [Revalski et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022ApJ...930...14R/abstract). Furthermore, the use of Si II* fine-structure transitions as a tool to measure gas electron densities ($n_e$) in outflows provides crucial constraints on properties like cloud size and volume filling factor [Xu et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...948...28X/abstract). Detailed observations such as those from the MAUVE survey highlight this complexity, revealing a spectacular 6 kpc bipolar ionized outflow in the Virgo cluster galaxy NGC 4383 that demonstrates complex kinematics and clumpy structure on 100 pc scales [Watts et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024MNRAS.530.1968W/abstract).

Conversely, [[molecular-outflows|Molecular outflows]] often dominate the total mass and momentum budget of the wind. Observations of [[star-forming-galaxies|dusty star-forming galaxies]] and ultra-luminous infrared galaxies (ULIRGs) show that the cold molecular phase can carry enormous amounts of material. The mass outflow rate for molecular gas in ULIRGs can reach up to $\sim 1200\ M_{\odot}\text{ yr}^{-1}$, vigorously depleting the star-forming fuel [Sturm et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011ApJ...733L..16S/abstract). Such massive molecular winds are ubiquitous, detected in over $70\%$ of massive, dusty star-forming galaxies at $z > 4$ [Spilker et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...905...85S/abstract). Further constraining this at low redshifts, the PHANGS-ALMA survey finds that 20-25% of nearby main-sequence disk galaxies host central molecular outflows; however, these flows are often found to be inefficient at quenching global star formation [Stuber et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021A&A...653A.172S/abstract). Interestingly, multi-wavelength studies have revealed that gamma-ray emission in star-forming galaxies strongly correlates with the presence of these molecular outflows, suggesting that these dense, multiphase systems act as highly efficient cosmic ray calorimeters [McDaniel et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...943..168M/abstract). High-resolution interferometry reveals that these molecular outflows possess a highly clumpy structure on $\sim 500$ pc scales. Different molecular tracers probe distinct density regimes: CO emission generally traces the diffuse molecular component, whereas HCN emission highlights dense gas clumps entrained within the flow [Spilker et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...905...85S/abstract), [Otter et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251209889O/abstract). Stellar feedback efficiently entrains dust within these cold and dense [[molecular-gas-and-cloud-evolution|molecular gas]] components of the wind, contributing significantly to observations of extraplanar dust [Kannan et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.503..336K/abstract).

The physical origin of this multiphase structure remains an active area of research. The cool and dense gas could be pre-existing interstellar medium clouds that are entrained and accelerated by the [[galactic-environmental-stripping|ram pressure]] of the hot wind fluid. Alternatively, fast-moving cool gas can form *in situ* within the outflow via catastrophic radiative cooling of the expanding hot wind [Schneider et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018ApJ...862...56S/abstract), [Gray et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019ApJ...887..161G/abstract).

The literature notes significant systematic discrepancies when characterizing this multiphase structure using different observational diagnostics. There is a well-documented tension in outflow properties derived from absorption versus emission lines. Absorption features generally probe higher velocities and larger spatial scales than emission lines [Scannapieco et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ApJ...837...28S/abstract). This discrepancy arises fundamentally from the density dependence of the tracers: emission-line luminosities scale with the square of the local gas density, thus heavily weighting compact, dense regions, while absorption-line depths scale linearly with column density, making them more sensitive to extended, diffuse, and high-velocity gas [Xu et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240919776X/abstract), [Xu et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ApJ...984...94X/abstract). For instance, findings from the CLASSY X project highlight a systemic discrepancy where empirical, partial-covering absorption-line models often severely underestimate column densities by neglecting large amounts of dense, low-velocity gas—components that are only adequately captured by higher-resolution semi-analytic modeling [Huberty et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240603646H/abstract). Consequently, combining multi-wavelength emission and absorption data is critical to achieving a complete physical accounting of galactic feedback.

## Chemical Enrichment and Metal Transport

Galactic outflows are the primary conduit for [[chemical-enrichment-and-metal-transport|Chemical Enrichment and Metal Transport]], transferring heavy elements from star-forming regions into the [[circumgalactic-medium|Circumgalactic Medium]] and the broader intergalactic medium (IGM) [Scannapieco et al. (2002)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2002ApJ...574..590S/abstract), [Barai et al. (2010)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011ApJ...727...54B/abstract). This transport process regulates the global baryon cycle and establishes the fundamental chemical scaling relations observed in galaxies across cosmic time.

In a [[multiphase-wind|Multiphase wind]], metals are not distributed equally among all thermal phases. Both localized high-resolution models and global cosmological simulations indicate that the hot phase ($T \approx 10^{6-7}$ K) of supernova-driven outflows carries the vast majority of the newly synthesized metals and thermal energy [Li et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...898..148L/abstract). The efficiency of this transport is parameterized by the metal-loading factor, often denoted $\eta_Z$, which represents the ratio of the metal mass outflow rate to the galactic metal production rate. Recent simulations suggest that the hot phase exhibits a tight scaling relationship between energy and metal loading, roughly $\eta_{E,h}/\eta_{Z,h} \sim 0.5$ [Li et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...890L..30L/abstract). At high redshifts ($z \sim 2-3$), outflows exhibit a distinct "chemical fingerprint" characterized by supersolar Si/Fe ratios; this strong alpha-enhancement alongside iron depletion onto dust grains clearly traces the specific nucleosynthetic yields of the driving starbursts [Jones et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018ApJ...863..191J/abstract). Overall, these winds are exceptionally efficient at high redshifts: nearly all metals produced by early star-forming galaxies are swept into outflows that reach beyond $0.25 R_{\rm vir}$, depositing a substantial fraction of the universe's metal budget directly into the CGM and IGM [Muratov et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017MNRAS.468.4170M/abstract).

The redistribution of these heavy elements dictates the shape of the global [[metallicity-distributions-and-scaling-relations|mass-metallicity relation]]. Because the specific binding energy of a galaxy scales proportionally to the square of its circular velocity ($V_c^2$), galaxies residing in shallow dark matter halos are highly susceptible to early metal loss. Dwarf galaxies experience significant metal-enriched outflows that permanently eject heavy elements, severely reducing their effective yield. Conversely, [[massive-galaxies|Massive galaxies]] with deep potential wells can retain their gas for extended periods, facilitating prolonged [[astration|Astration]] and resulting in higher mean stellar metallicities. This mass-dependent retention mechanism naturally explains why the mass-metallicity relation reaches a plateau at halo masses of $\log (M_{\rm halo}/M_\odot) \gtrsim 12$, above which even hot outflows lack the specific energy to permanently escape [Li et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...890L..30L/abstract).

Differential mass loss across a galactic disk also plays a crucial role in establishing the [[galactic-metal-abundance-gradient|Galactic metal abundance gradient]]. While earlier models relying purely on reduced gas inflow rates produced negative [[abundance-gradients|Abundance gradients]] that were too steep compared to the data (e.g., $\Delta[Z/H]/\Delta \log r \sim -0.5$), the introduction of [[selective-galactic-winds|differential galactic winds]] successfully reproduces the shallower observed gradients. Because the local escape velocity decreases with increasing galactocentric radius, galactic winds are preferentially launched from the outer disk regions earlier in the galaxy's evolutionary history. The premature onset of these winds truncates local star formation and halts further chemical enrichment in the outskirts, naturally producing the observed shallow negative abundance profiles.

Finally, [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]] heavily influences the spatial distribution of metals on the largest scales. AGN-driven outflows enrich the [[hot-circumgalactic-medium|Hot circumgalactic medium]] in an "inside-out" fashion by lofting centrally produced metals to large radii via buoyant bubbles and jets. This process flattens the metallicity profiles of massive halos, elevating the iron abundance to $Z_{\rm Fe} \approx 0.23 Z_{\rm Fe,\odot}$ at half the virial radius ($0.5 R_{500}$) [Choi et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...904....8C/abstract). Once deposited in the halo, this metal-rich gas cools much more efficiently than primordial gas, facilitating [[wind-recycling|Wind recycling]]—a critical mechanism where previously ejected metals rain back onto the disk to fuel late-time star formation.

## Baryonic Cycling and Wind Recycling

The evolution of galaxies is tightly coupled to the continuous exchange of gas between the interstellar medium and the [[circumgalactic-medium|Circumgalactic Medium]] (CGM). Galactic outflows act as the primary transport mechanism in this baryon cycle, ejecting mass, metals, and energy into the halo and beyond. Understanding the exact origin of this entrained material is an evolving field; for example, recent findings from HI4PI data suggest that cold gas in [[the-galactic-center|Galactic Center]] outflows is stripped from bar-driven dust lanes and streams at $R \sim 0.5-1.7$ kpc rather than originating solely from the [[central-molecular-zone|Central Molecular Zone]] [Su et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251214081S/abstract). For instance, the Galactic Center lobe provides a spectacular local, 100-pc scale example of a magnetized, dusty starburst outflow, serving as an accessible analog to the large-scale multiphase winds observed in distant dwarf galaxies [Law et al. (2009)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010ApJ...708..474L/abstract).

Rather than escaping the dark matter halo entirely, a substantial fraction of the ejected gas remains gravitationally bound. In the [[galactic-fountains|Galactic fountains]] model, this heated gas is pushed into the lower halo, where it accumulates, cools, and eventually re-accretes onto the galactic disk. This process, known as [[wind-recycling|Wind recycling]], is a critical mechanism for maintaining late-time star formation by providing steady [[net-gas-inflows|Net gas inflows]] after a galaxy's initial cold gas reservoirs are depleted [van de Voort et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ASSL..430..301V/abstract). This continuous exchange establishes a complex cycle that can also give rise to a "wind pileup" scenario. Cosmological simulations (e.g., the FIRE project) suggest that as a galaxy transitions to a smoother mode of late-time star formation, previously ejected material forms a dense gas reservoir in the inner CGM that subsequently cools to fuel compact central starbursts and luminous quasars [Mercedes-Feliz et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251019905M/abstract).

Ejected material is naturally metal-enriched compared to the primordial accreting gas. Because metal-line cooling is highly efficient, the elevated metallicity of the outflowing gas significantly shortens its cooling timescale, thereby accelerating its re-accretion rate [van de Voort et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ASSL..430..301V/abstract). High-resolution simulations demonstrate that nearly all metals produced by high-redshift galaxies are initially carried into the [[circumgalactic-medium|Circumgalactic Medium]] by winds [Muratov et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017MNRAS.468.4170M/abstract). For [[massive-galaxies|Milky Way-mass halos]], hot supernova-driven outflows establish a large-scale, metal-enriched atmosphere where the condensation of cool gas continuously balances the injection of new hot material [Li et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...898..148L/abstract).

Furthermore, [[stellar-and-agn-feedback|Stellar and AGN Feedback]] both contribute heavily to this global cycle. Active galactic nuclei (AGN) winds in particular enrich the halo "inside-out," spreading centrally produced metals out to the virial radius and beyond, flattening the overall metallicity profile. In group-scale halos, for instance, simulated AGN feedback drives the circumgalactic iron abundance to $Z_{\rm Fe} \approx 0.23 Z_{{\rm Fe},\odot}$ at a radius of $0.5 R_{500}$ [Choi et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...904....8C/abstract). On even larger scales, these outflows are responsible for early intergalactic medium (IGM) enrichment. The initial IGM pollution is generally incomplete and inhomogeneous, heavily biased toward regions surrounding early starbursts; simulations indicate that at most $30\%$ of the IGM volume is enriched above $10^{-3} Z_\odot$ by early winds [Scannapieco et al. (2002)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2002ApJ...574..590S/abstract). Globally, galactic outflows raise the mass-averaged IGM metallicity to $[{\rm O}/{\rm H}] \approx -5$ at $z=5.5$ and $[{\rm O}/{\rm H}] \approx -2.8$ by $z=0$ [Barai et al. (2010)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011ApJ...727...54B/abstract).

While the qualitative picture of the baryon cycle is well established, the quantitative efficiency of [[wind-recycling|Wind recycling]] versus permanent gas escape remains a subject of active debate. The literature is currently conflicting, as the fraction of gas that successfully re-accretes is highly sensitive to the adopted subgrid feedback implementations in cosmological simulations [van de Voort et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ASSL..430..301V/abstract). For example, some models suggest that a large fraction of the mass ejected from halos with $M_{\rm h} \le 10^{12} M_\odot$ never returns, leaving these low-mass systems permanently baryon-deficient compared to the cosmic mean at $z=0$ [Muratov et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015MNRAS.454.2691M/abstract). Similarly, analytical treatments of entropy-driven winds show that they can produce long wind recycling times [Keller et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.493.2149K/abstract), further complicating attempts to precisely constrain the [[net-gas-inflows|Net gas inflows]] required to sustain equilibrium star formation across different galactic environments.

## Regulation of Star Formation: Positive and Negative Feedback

The evolution of galaxies is fundamentally governed by the interplay between gas accretion and feedback. Once gas falls into the galactic potential well, feedback processes—driven by massive stars and AGNs—act in two opposing modes: [[negative-feedback|Negative feedback]], which suppresses star formation by depleting or heating gas, and [[positive-feedback-astrophysics|Positive feedback (astrophysics)]], which triggers or enhances star formation through localized gas compression.

As previously established, the implementation of [[self-regulated-feedback-mechanisms|Self-regulated feedback mechanisms]] is essential to curb runaway star formation [Hopkins et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011MNRAS.417..950H/abstract), [Agertz et al. (2014)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015ApJ...804...18A/abstract). In low-mass dwarf galaxies, stellar feedback drastically reduces the star formation efficiency [Emerick et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018ApJ...865L..22E/abstract), [Chevance et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022MNRAS.509..272C/abstract). In [[massive-galaxies|Massive galaxies]], mechanical and radiative energy from AGN prevents catastrophic cooling [Ciotti et al. (2010)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010ApJ...717..708C/abstract), [Fabian et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012ARA&A..50..455F/abstract). Observationally, [[active-post-starburst-galaxies|massive post-starburst galaxies]] at $z \sim 0.6$ show fossil galactic winds with velocities up to $2000 \text{ km s}^{-1}$, potentially linked to the rapid quenching of star formation by an [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|AGN]]. However, expanding superbubbles, outflows, and jets can conversely induce star formation by sweeping up and compressing dense cold gas clouds until they undergo gravitational collapse. 

This [[positive-feedback-astrophysics|positive feedback]] is frequently observed in gas-rich environments and systems hosting radio jets. For example, radio-selected AGNs exhibit systematically higher star formation rates than X-ray-selected AGNs at a given luminosity, strongly suggesting jet-induced star formation [Zinn et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013ApJ...774...66Z/abstract). High-resolution hydrodynamical simulations demonstrate that the overpressurization of a galactic disk by an AGN can boost the global star formation rate by $\sim 25\%$ to a full order of magnitude, driving significant gas fragmentation in starburst dwarf galaxies [Bieri et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016MNRAS.455.4166B/abstract), [Su et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251020897S/abstract). Observationally, spatially resolved integral field spectroscopy of local Seyfert galaxies, such as NGC 5728, reveals that AGN-driven outflows impacting star-forming rings can elevate local star formation rate surface densities to $\sim 1.8 \ M_\odot \ \mathrm{yr}^{-1} \ \mathrm{kpc}^{-2}$. The corresponding depletion of CO emission in these compressed regions indicates exceptionally high star formation efficiencies in the shocked gas [Shin et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019ApJ...881..147S/abstract).

Despite clear detections of positive feedback on local scales, the literature remains conflicted over its global impact on stellar mass assembly. It is actively debated whether positive feedback can significantly alter the integrated stellar mass of a galaxy, or if it merely represents a localized, short-lived effect before negative feedback dominates and quenches the system. However, recent semi-analytic frameworks, such as the FEGA model, incorporate treatments of positive feedback demonstrating that AGN-induced bursts of star formation actively improve the accuracy of predicted stellar mass functions and associated scaling relations [Contini et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJS..274...41C/abstract). Furthermore, recent theoretical frameworks suggest a cosmic transition in the dominant feedback mode: feedback in the very early universe ($z > 6$) may have been predominantly positive, stimulating vigorous early star formation through outflow-induced turbulence, before shifting to the energy-conserving, gas-depleting negative feedback that characterizes late-time massive galaxies [Silk et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...961L..39S/abstract).

## Historical Development of Feedback Models

The theoretical understanding of galaxy formation initially centered on monolithic collapse, which predicted steep [[abundance-gradients|metallicity gradients]] (e.g., $\Delta[Z/H]/\Delta\log r \sim -1$). To reconcile these models with observations, early theorists postulated that galactic winds driven by supernovae could heat the interstellar medium and remove metal-enriched gas, particularly in the shallower potential wells of low-mass galaxies. As the paradigm shifted toward hierarchical formation, models faced the severe [[overcooling-problem|Overcooling problem]]. In cold dark matter cosmologies, gas in small halos at high redshift cools highly efficiently, predicting a present-day stellar mass density ($\Omega_{\star, 0} \simeq \Omega_{b,0}$) that violently contradicts observational data.

To resolve this discrepancy, the [[sn-feedback-model|SN feedback model]] became a foundational component in cosmological simulations. For instance, a feedback-halting experiment in [[massive-galaxies|Milky Way-mass]] FIRE-2 simulations demonstrated that abruptly removing feedback causes turbulent velocities to decay and the global star formation rate to surge by over an order of magnitude, directly illustrating the dynamic necessity of feedback [Khullar et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...973...40K/abstract). Because early simulations could not resolve individual supernovae, they relied on heuristic subgrid models to inject thermal or kinetic energy into the [[cosmic-media-and-interstellar-medium|Cosmic Media and Interstellar Medium]]. A major theoretical paradigm shift occurred when high-resolution hydrodynamic simulations (e.g., FIRE-2 and SMUGGLE) demonstrated that supernova feedback alone is insufficient if the energy is injected directly into dense, rapid-cooling gas. It is now understood that pre-supernova feedback—such as stellar ionizing radiation and winds—is critical to clear dense molecular clouds, allowing subsequent supernova energy to couple efficiently and drive large-scale outflows [Emerick et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018ApJ...865L..22E/abstract), [Li et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.499.5862L/abstract). In this context, theorists developed universal scaling relations for superbubble evolution (e.g., the Osaka model), which emphasizes the necessity of combining both thermal and mechanical feedback to adequately suppress star formation [Oku et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022ApJS..262....9O/abstract). Despite these theoretical advancements, significant ambiguity remains in the literature regarding the exact coupling efficiency of this energy. Cosmological simulations often require a high [[mass-loading-factor|Mass loading factor]] ($\eta \sim 10-100$) in dwarf galaxies to reproduce the stellar mass function, whereas some recent observations find values as low as $\eta \sim 0.02$, indicating a gentle gas cycle rather than violent, galaxy-wide blow-outs [Marasco et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023A&A...670A..92M/abstract).

While [[stellar-and-agn-feedback|Stellar and AGN Feedback]] are both critical, stellar feedback alone fails to halt star formation in massive halos ($M \gtrsim 10^{12} M_\odot$). Consequently, models introduced energy injection from [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]] to prevent overcooling and maintain quenching in massive ellipticals [Fabian et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012ARA&A..50..455F/abstract), [King et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015ARA&A..53..115K/abstract). This dual-feedback approach led to the proposal of a broader evolutionary sequence linking starbursts and quasars: beginning with a heavily dust-obscured ultra-luminous infrared galaxy, radiation pressure on dust expels the obscuring cocoon in a blow-out event, eventually revealing an unobscured optical quasar [Ishibashi et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016MNRAS.463.1291I/abstract). 

Historically, theorists treated AGN feedback primarily as a monotonic, instantaneous quenching mechanism ([[negative-feedback|Negative feedback]]). However, contemporary literature highlights a much more complex reality. Observations show that AGN frequently reside in gas-rich, star-forming galaxies, implying that global quenching is significantly delayed and requires multiple cumulative episodes to take effect [Harrison et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024IAUS..378...57H/abstract). Furthermore, models and observations increasingly support [[positive-feedback-astrophysics|Positive feedback (astrophysics)]], wherein AGN jets or supernova-driven shocks compress dense gas and trigger localized starbursts rather than simply expelling fuel [Zinn et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013ApJ...774...66Z/abstract), [Su et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251020897S/abstract). Recent insights suggest that feedback in the early universe ($z > 6$) may have been predominantly positive, only transitioning to dominant negative feedback at later cosmic epochs [Silk et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...961L..39S/abstract).

## Scaling Relations and Mass Loading

The efficiency of gas expulsion in galaxies is typically parameterized by the [[mass-loading-factor|Mass loading factor]] (or [[wind-mass-loading|Wind mass loading]]), defined as the ratio of the mass outflow rate to the star formation rate: $\eta = \dot{M}_{\rm out}/\mathrm{SFR}$. This dimensionless quantity describes the rate at which baryons are removed from the interstellar medium relative to their consumption by star formation. Cosmological simulations universally require $\eta \gg 1$ in low-mass halos to reproduce the observed stellar mass function, prevent runaway star formation, and avoid the [[overcooling-problem|Overcooling problem]] [Muratov et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015MNRAS.454.2691M/abstract), [Huang et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.493....1H/abstract).

Theoretical models of momentum-conserving winds predict that the mass loading factor should scale with the circular velocity of the galaxy as $\eta \propto V_c^{-1}$ [Hopkins et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012MNRAS.421.3522H/abstract), [Sugahara et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ApJ...850...51S/abstract). Furthermore, scaling relations for different gas phases reveal nuanced behaviors; for instance, ionized wind mass outflow rates scale more steeply with AGN bolometric luminosity than molecular rates, suggesting the two phases may converge at high AGN luminosities [Fiore et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017A&A...601A.143F/abstract). In starburst environments, observations from the CLASSY survey indicate that warm ionized outflows carry only $\sim 20\%$ of the newly synthesized silicon, with their mass-loading factors scaling inversely with circular velocity exhibiting a log-log slope of roughly $-1.6$ [Xu et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022ApJ...933..222X/abstract). Cosmological hydrodynamical simulations often find similar or steeper relationships. For example, the EAGLE simulations find $\eta \propto V_c^{-3/2}$ in the low-mass regime where stellar feedback processes dominate [Mitchell et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.494.3971M/abstract), while other models require scalings as steep as $\eta \propto \sigma^5$ to match high-redshift stellar mass functions [Huang et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.493....1H/abstract). In simulated dwarf galaxies, $\eta$ routinely reaches values of 10-100 [Muratov et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015MNRAS.454.2691M/abstract), [Andersson et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023MNRAS.521.2196A/abstract). However, a significant tension exists with direct observations: integral field spectroscopy of nearby starburst dwarf galaxies has measured mass loading factors as low as $\eta \sim 0.02$, approximately two orders of magnitude lower than the theoretical requirements for global feedback, suggesting that stellar feedback in these environments may stimulate a gentle gas cycle rather than large-scale blow-outs [Marasco et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023A&A...670A..92M/abstract).

Outflow kinematics also exhibit strong correlations with the global star formation rate. Systematics of optical absorption lines demonstrate that the maximum outflow velocity scales approximately as $v_{\rm wind} \propto \mathrm{SFR}^{0.3}$ [Weiner et al. (2008)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2009ApJ...692..187W/abstract), [Sugahara et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ApJ...850...51S/abstract). In extreme environments, such as local ultra-luminous infrared galaxies, molecular mass outflow rates can exceed $1200 M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ [Sturm et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011ApJ...733L..16S/abstract). Furthermore, outflow properties exhibit clear redshift evolution; at a given SFR, outflow velocities are observed to increase by $0.05{-}0.3$ dex from $z=0$ to $z=2$ [Sugahara et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ApJ...850...51S/abstract). The mass loading factor itself is inferred to evolve with redshift, scaling roughly as $\eta \propto (1+z)^{1.2\pm0.3}$ at a fixed circular velocity [Sugahara et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ApJ...850...51S/abstract).

As galaxy mass increases, the deeper gravitational potential limits the ability of star formation to drive global winds. Near a halo mass of $\sim 10^{12} M_\odot$, an upturn in the mass loading factor is required to halt star formation, signaling the onset of [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]] as the dominant feedback mechanism in [[massive-galaxies|Massive galaxies]] [Mitchell et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.494.3971M/abstract). Feedback from these central supermassive black holes generates powerful, high-velocity winds that link the black hole mass to the bulge velocity dispersion. This mechanism is critical for establishing the observed $M-\sigma$ relation [Fabian et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012ARA&A..50..455F/abstract), [Zubovas et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019GReGr..51...65Z/abstract). Interestingly, advanced hydrodynamic models indicate that while improved AGN feedback treatments are essential for galaxy quenching, they mostly control the dispersion around these black hole-stellar mass scaling relations rather than fundamentally shaping their underlying slopes [Menci et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023A&A...674A.181M/abstract). At these mass scales, momentum- and energy-driven AGN outflows are necessary to clear dense circum-nuclear gas reservoirs and prevent further overcooling [King et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015ARA&A..53..115K/abstract).

## Open Questions and Future Frontiers

Despite the central role of [[stellar-and-agn-feedback|Stellar and AGN Feedback]] in modern cosmological models, the physical mechanisms that drive and regulate galactic outflows remain a subject of intense active debate. 

A primary theoretical uncertainty is the exact **coupling efficiency** of mechanical and radiative energy to the multiphase interstellar medium. Cosmological simulations require high [[mass-loading-factor|Mass loading factor]]s ($\eta \sim 10-100$) in dwarf galaxies to prevent the [[overcooling-problem|Overcooling problem]] and reproduce the observed stellar mass function [Huang et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.493....1H/abstract). However, this theoretically mandated efficiency conflicts with recent integral-field observations of nearby starburst dwarfs, which infer mass loading factors as low as $\eta \sim 0.02$. Such findings suggest that stellar feedback may stimulate a gentle local gas cycle rather than the massive, galaxy-wide blowouts predicted by simulations [Marasco et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023A&A...670A..92M/abstract). 

The thermodynamic evolution of outflowing gas also presents a major theoretical frontier. The standard adiabatic superwind model is complicated by the fact that hot, supernova-driven winds may undergo **catastrophic cooling**. This rapid cooling suppresses adiabatic expansion and shifts the energy budget, generating non-equilibrium ionization states and strong nebular emission lines (e.g., C IV, O VI, He II) that can drastically alter the interpretation of observational diagnostics [Gray et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019ApJ...887..161G/abstract). Detailed modeling of non-equilibrium chemistry in steady-state outflows has shown that these conditions can successfully reproduce observed O VI and N V column density ratios, standing in stark contrast to traditional assumptions of photoionization equilibrium [Gray et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019ApJ...875..110G/abstract). Furthermore, the role of cosmic rays as an additional feedback pressure component is actively debated; it remains unclear whether cosmic rays reliably drive large-scale [[astrophysical-outflows-and-jets|Astrophysical Outflows and Jets]] or if they primarily redirect energy into localized recycling flows [Owen et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250916524O/abstract). Recent cosmological zoom-in simulations emphasize that cosmic ray feedback is highly mass-dependent; it significantly suppresses star formation and reduces gas half-mass radii primarily in lower-mass galaxies (halos below $10^{12} M_\odot$), whereas its impact diminishes in more massive systems [Bieri et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250907124B/abstract). Recent modeling efforts indicate that producing cosmic rays at jet cocoon shock fronts—rather than injecting them immediately near the central black hole—more effectively suppresses cooling flows by sustaining a high jet energy flux for longer durations [Su et al. (2026)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2026MNRAS.545f2060S/abstract).

In the regime of [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]], the simple paradigm of monotonic "[[negative-feedback|negative feedback]]"—where AGN rapidly expel gas and immediately quench star formation—is heavily challenged. Observations show that AGN frequently reside in gas-rich galaxies without instantaneous global quenching, suggesting a significant temporal delay in the impact of AGN outflows [Woo et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ApJ...839..120W/abstract), [Luo et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021ApJ...908..221L/abstract). Additionally, literature is conflicted regarding the prevalence of [[positive-feedback-astrophysics|Positive feedback (astrophysics)]]. High-resolution models and targeted observations indicate that AGN-driven shocks and radio jets can compress dense gas, enhancing the star formation rate rather than suppressing it, especially in gas-rich dwarf galaxies and radio-loud AGN [Zinn et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013ApJ...774...66Z/abstract), [Su et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251020897S/abstract). Additionally, recent integral field unit (IFU) detections of fast, AGN-driven outflows in dwarf galaxies, reaching velocities up to $1200 \text{ km s}^{-1}$, indicate that these winds may escape the host and significantly enrich the [[circumgalactic-medium|CGM]], further complicating our understanding of supermassive black hole feedback in low-mass halos [Liu et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...905..166L/abstract).

Resolving these tensions requires mapping the multiphase kinematics of outflows across a wider range of cosmic time and spatial scales. In the radio and millimeter regimes, the proposed **ngVLA** will revolutionize our understanding by resolving low-power radio jet-ISM interactions on scales of a few parsecs and tracing the cold molecular phase of outflows via low-$J$ CO transitions [Nyland et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018ApJ...859...23N/abstract), [Spilker et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018arXiv181006605S/abstract). Concurrently, **JWST diagnostics** are extending feedback studies into the Epoch of Reionization. Early JWST observations have already detected exceptionally fast [O III] outflows reaching velocities up to $\sim 8400$ km s$^{-1}$ in luminous $z \sim 5-6$ quasars [Liu et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250908793L/abstract). These next-generation facilities will be critical in determining whether early-universe feedback transitioned from a predominantly positive, turbulence-driven phase to the energy-conserving, negative feedback modes that govern massive galaxies today [Silk et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...961L..39S/abstract).

>   - Incorporate the FEGA25 model's coordination of negative, positive, and hot gas-ejection modes, which expels gas beyond the virial radius to match observed halo gas fractions.
> - [Outflows in the gaseous disks of active galaxies and their impact on black hole scaling relations](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023A&A...674A.181M/abstract) (`2023A&A...674A.181M`)
>   - Suggested section: *Scaling Relations and Mass Loading*
>   - Note that improved AGN feedback treatments mostly control the dispersion around BH-stellar mass scaling relations rather than fundamentally shaping their slopes.
> - [The failure of stellar feedback, magnetic fields, conduction, and morphological quenching in maintaining red galaxies](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019MNRAS.487.4393S/abstract) (`2019MNRAS.487.4393S`)
>   - Suggested section: *Fundamental Drivers: Stellar and AGN Feedback*
>   - Mention that non-AGN mechanisms like Type Ia supernovae, cosmic rays, and morphological quenching are insufficient to halt cooling flows in halos above 10^12 solar masses.
> - [MAGNUM survey: Compact jets causing large turmoil in galaxies. Enhanced line widths perpendicular to radio jets as tracers of jet-ISM interaction](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021A&A...648A..17V/abstract) (`2021A&A...648A..17V`)
>   - Suggested section: *AGN Feedback: Quasar and Radio Modes*
>   - Discuss how low-power jets can drive significant ionized gas turmoil and shocks perpendicular to the jet axis, as observed in the MAGNUM survey.
> - [Frequency and nature of central molecular outflows in nearby star-forming disk galaxies](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021A&A...653A.172S/abstract) (`2021A&A...653A.172S`)
>   - Suggested section: *Multiphase Outflow Structure*
>   - Incorporate the PHANGS-ALMA finding that 20-25% of nearby main-sequence galaxies host central molecular outflows, though these are often inefficient at quenching global star formation.
> - [Gamma-Ray Emission from Galaxies Hosting Molecular Outflows](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...943..168M/abstract) (`2023ApJ...943..168M`)
>   - Suggested section: *Multiphase Outflow Structure*
>   - Add that gamma-ray emission in star-forming galaxies correlates with molecular outflows, suggesting these systems act as efficient cosmic ray calorimeters.
> - [Dust in the Wind: Composition and Kinematics of Galaxy Outflows at the Peak Epoch of Star Formation](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018ApJ...863..191J/abstract) (`2018ApJ...863..191J`)
>   - Suggested section: *Chemical Enrichment and Metal Transport*
>   - Mention the 'chemical fingerprint' of outflows at z~2-3, characterized by supersolar Si/Fe ratios indicating alpha-enhancement and dust depletion.
> - [A Multiwavelength View of a Mass Outflow from the Galactic Center](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010ApJ...708..474L/abstract) (`2010ApJ...708..474L`)
>   - Suggested section: *Baryonic Cycling and Wind Recycling*
>   - Include the Galactic Center lobe as a local 100-pc scale example of a magnetized, dusty starburst outflow analogous to those in dwarf galaxies.
> - [CLASSY X: Highlighting Differences Between Partial Covering and Semi-Analytic Modeling in the Estimate of Galactic Outflow Properties](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240603646H/abstract) (`2024arXiv240603646H`)
>   - Suggested section: *Multiphase Outflow Structure*
>   - Note the systemic discrepancy where empirical absorption-line models may underestimate column densities by neglecting large amounts of dense, low-velocity gas detectable only by higher-resolution semi-analytic models.
> - [Unveiling the Impact of Cosmic Rays on the Disc Sizes and Outflows from Dwarf Scales to Galaxy Groups](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250907124B/abstract) (`2025arXiv250907124B`)
>   - Suggested section: *Open Questions and Future Frontiers*
>   - Highlight that cosmic ray feedback significantly suppresses star formation and reduces gas half-mass radii primarily in lower-mass galaxies below 10^12 solar masses.
